title: ADHD pt 2
summary: Part two of the ADHD double episode. Hosts cover how ADHD is diagnosed (inattentive and hyperactive symptom checklists, the role of parent and teacher input, cost and psychiatrist shortages), risk factors (heredity, pregnancy issues, lead exposure, screen time as a link rather than cause), prevalence figures across the US and other countries and the doubling of diagnoses, adult ADHD and how it is often missed (especially in girls), comorbidities such as autism, depression, anxiety, and oppositional defiant disorder, empathy, false memories, masking and its effects on self-esteem and relationships, injury and divorce risk, addiction and homelessness, treatment options (medication including stimulants, coaching, therapy, exercise, family training), and resources. Listener mail is skipped.

entities.name: Journal of the American Medical Association

segments.title: Opening and series heads-up
segments.summary: Josh gives a heads-up that this two-part episode covers adult-oriented ADHD topics and suggests parents preview it before sharing with kids. The show intro plays.

segments.title: Hereditary risk and causes of ADHD
segments.summary: Chuck explains that heredity is the biggest factor, with a roughly fifty percent chance a child of a parent with ADHD has it. Josh lists other risk factors: pregnancy issues like alcohol or tobacco exposure, premature birth, low birth weight, childhood lead exposure, and brain injury. Research on blue dyes No. 1 and No. 2 may worsen symptoms.

segments.title: Screen time and ADHD
segments.summary: The hosts clarify that TV and screens do not cause ADHD, but kids with ADHD are drawn to screens for dopamine. A large study of five-year-olds found heavy TV watchers had much higher odds of meeting ADHD criteria.

segments.title: Diagnosing ADHD
segments.summary: Diagnosis is complicated for young children because other developmental issues can mimic ADHD. Differential factors include learning disabilities, mood disorders, vision or hearing problems, and sleep disorders. The DSM criteria use inattentive and hyperactive lists of nine items each, with six needed for kids and five for adults. Diagnosis combines school records, parent reports, and teacher input, and Chuck describes how parent-teacher conferences help. Josh warns about misleading TikTok diagnostic tests.

segments.title: Cost and access to ADHD diagnosis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how often diagnosis is unaffordable or delayed. Psychiatrist shortages, long waitlists, and the need for a specialist make the process costlier, and psychiatrists typically charge more than therapists. Many cases likely go undiagnosed.

segments.title: ADHD prevalence and diagnosis rates worldwide
segments.summary: US children aged three to seventeen have about a ten percent diagnosis rate, with boys at about thirteen percent versus six percent for girls. Rates vary by race: twelve percent for Black children, ten for White, eight for Hispanic, and three for Asian children. A 2017 global study found about five point three percent of children. Diagnoses in the US doubled between 2005 and 2014, and the DSM-5 changed criteria in 2013. Younger-for-grade children can be misdiagnosed, and COVID schooling disruption complicates evaluation. Josh gives figures for the UK, Australia, Canada, and Germany.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break with a short sponsor segment.

segments.title: ADHD in adults and outgrowing it
segments.summary: Adult ADHD rates vary widely across studies. A 2021 study found about nine percent of those diagnosed as kids had fully recovered by young adulthood, though there is no known cure. Adults often show disorganization, mood swings, procrastination, and misdiagnosis as anxiety or depression. Girls often mask symptoms and are missed until adulthood.
topics: ADHD misdiagnosis as depression or anxiety

segments.title: Comorbidities: autism, depression, anxiety, and ODD
segments.summary: Thirty to eighty percent of people with autism are also diagnosed with ADHD, and twenty to fifty percent of people with ADHD have autism. ADHD is more common than autism. Kids with ADHD are about five times likelier to have depression, and about forty percent of kids have anxiety. Thirty to fifty percent meet criteria for oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder. The hosts discuss a child kicking a seat on a plane and the empathy that parents and others can offer.

segments.title: ADHD and empathy
segments.summary: Josh explains that people with ADHD often have low emotional or cognitive empathy, which can reduce connections, though they do care. Chuck notes that empathy grows with life experience.

segments.title: False memories and relationships
segments.summary: Studies show kids with ADHD are more likely to remember items that were not on a list and to defend those false memories. Josh explains how this can lead to unintentional gaslighting and arguments in relationships. Chuck and Josh note that close relationships can be deeper because of the trust they require.

segments.title: Injury risk and ADHD sway
segments.summary: Adults with ADHD are about twice as likely to be injured. The hosts describe ADHD sway, a postural imbalance associated with ADHD, and a viral video about walking beside someone with ADHD.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break with a short sponsor segment.

segments.title: Masking, self-esteem, and family life
segments.summary: Josh defines masking as camouflaging symptoms to fit in, which is sometimes necessary but can erode self-esteem and self-compassion. Chuck connects masking to fatigue and mood swings. Lower parental warmth toward kids with ADHD, especially maternal warmth, is noted, and adults with ADHD are about twice as likely to divorce. Josh adds that people with ADHD face higher addiction risk, and that a quarter of people in US treatment programs and between 24 and 62 percent of homeless people in the US were found to have ADHD.

segments.title: ADHD treatment: medication, therapy, and family training
segments.summary: Chuck notes that ADHD is highly treatable, with coaching, therapy, and medication. In 2016, sixty-two percent of diagnosed US kids were on medication. Josh explains that stimulants such as Adderall, Vyvanse, and Strattera are the usual first-line drugs, and that research has not found addiction in kids on stimulants. Chuck describes immediate and extended release forms and non-stimulant options such as clonidine. A 2023 JAMA study found increased cardiovascular risk from long-term stimulant use in a Swedish cohort. Family training and authoritative parenting are described as helpful.

segments.title: Exercise, coaching, and organizational systems
segments.summary: Exercise can increase dopamine and help executive functioning. Coaching focuses on practical strategies such as time management, and phone calendars and reminders are recommended. Chuck stresses the importance of systems.

segments.title: Treatment outcomes and resources
segments.summary: A 2012 meta-analysis of 351 English-language studies found seventy-two percent of treated people had improved long-term outcomes. The hosts recommend resources including Melissa Orlov, Gina Perla, Russell Barkley, Sasha Hamdani, and Instagram accounts. They caution listeners about social media advice.

segments.title: Outro and listener contact
segments.summary: Chuck closes by encouraging empathy and skips listener mail. Josh shares an email address for contact, and the show credits are read.
